newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia T-bill tax seen boon for foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: Russia T-bill tax seen boon for foreign investors.

text.p: New taxes on Russian government securities could be good news for foreign investors, fixed income analysts and government officials said on Tuesday.
But the final impact of the legislation will depend to a large extent on how it is applied, they said, noting that many details have not yet been clarified.
The law, which took effect on Tuesday and applies to new issues only, imposes a 43 percent tax rate on profits on government securities for banks and a 35 percent rate for others.
But some foreign investors are exempt from double taxation under existing tax treaties and they will probably win out, analysts and officials said.
Russian Central Bank Deputy Chairman Andrei Kozlov told Reuters that tax treaties would probably keep real tax rates flat for most non-residents.

"I imagine non-residents will pay more attention to new issues (to which the taxes apply) -- the nominal yield will be higher in any case, and taxation treaties will allow them to make a bigger profit," he said.
Kozlov said he expected guidelines for the application of the tax to be published on Tuesday and analysts said these could offset the effect of taxation treaties.

"It's all in the details," said a Western fund manager, who said non-resident investors could make a substantial profit at the expense of the Russian budget. "Whoever understands this first stands to make a lot of money."

Fixed income analysts said that Russians, who hold most of the GKO discount Treasury bills and OFZ government bonds, would face sharply higher real tax rates, and yields would rise to reflect that new tax rate.
Banks, which are charged the highest rate, are the largest holder of Russian T-bills.
Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Troika-Dialog bank in Moscow, said the higher yields could hurt the Russian treasury.

"It appears the government will pay more in supporting higher yields than it will gain from higher taxes on government securities profits," he said. Yields, currently just over 30 percent, could break through 50 percent on the change, he said.
The Russian parliament passed the amendment, affecting T-bills and bonds which had been free of tax, as part of a package of laws to help fund the 1997 budget.
The law will apply to securities issued on Wednesday at the regular government auction and one operator said some bids were likely to be extremely low to test the new situation.
The fund manager said the new law appeared to allow deductions for expenses against tax payments which could make Russian T-bills attractive to businesses looking for tax hedges.
"It could change the form of the market," he said.
One fixed income analyst said the government had made a mistake by giving non-government investors the edge. "This is federally sanctioned capital flight," the analyst said.
